sections.h2: What is Canyon County, Idaho, like for a homeowner?
sections.html:
Canyon County is part of the Boise metropolitan area, west of Ada County, with Caldwell as the county seat and Nampa as its largest city. Wikipedia gives the area as 604 square miles, about 587 of them land, and lists Ada, Payette, Gem and Owyhee counties and Malheur County, Oregon, as neighbors.

The Idaho Legislature created the county from Ada County in an act approved March 7, 1891. It once held all of what became Payette County and part of Gem County. Middleton was the first European settlement, from 1863, and the railroad's arrival at Caldwell led to a town there by August 1883. Nampa was platted in 1886.

Nine cities are in the county, one of them only in part:

  • Caldwell, Nampa, Middleton and Parma
  • Greenleaf, Melba, Notus and Wilder
  • Star, mostly in Ada County

Roads are Interstate 84, US 20, 26, 30 and 95, and state highways 19, 44, 45 and 55. Part of the Deer Flat National Wildlife Refuge lies inside the county. The levy table later on this page shows that a city levy is one component of the bill, so the taxing districts listed on your notice matter.

sections.h2: How does the Canyon County economy affect home sellers?
sections.html:
The county's 2025 covered employment of 89,966 is led by trade, transportation and utilities (21,409), education and health services (19,006), construction (11,968) and manufacturing (10,869). The Idaho Department of Labor counts a 2025 population of 275,123, a 2024 median household income of $76,488 and a June 2026 unemployment rate of 3.7%.

Commuting is a defining feature. In 2023 an estimated 49,391 workers lived and worked in Canyon County, 38,578 came in from other counties and 65,317 residents left the county for work. Boise was the most common workplace for residents, at 29,863 jobs, ahead of Nampa at 27,427.

sections.h2: Who handles property tax in Canyon County?
sections.html:
Two elected offices split the work: the Assessor values the property and the Treasurer bills and collects. Canyon County's Assessor office says plainly that the Treasurer sends tax bills, receives payments and distributes the money to taxing districts.

  • Assessor: 111 N. 11th Ave, Suite 250, Caldwell; 208-454-7431; 2cAsr@canyoncounty.id.gov.
  • Treasurer: 111 N. 11th Ave, Suite 240, Caldwell; 208-454-7354; treas@canyoncounty.id.gov.
  • Board of Equalization: the County Commissioners, who must finish their business and adjourn by the second Monday in July.

Under Idaho Code 63-205, the assessed value must match actual market value as of January 1. The county reappraises every property on a five-year cycle and trends values in the years between. Its published guidance stresses that taxes are budget driven, not assessment driven, and that local budgets face a 3% cap plus new construction value. A single home can therefore see its bill rise even when its own value is flat.

sections.h2: How is a Canyon County tax bill calculated?
sections.html:
The bill is taxable value times the combined levy rate of every district that serves the property. The Assessor's site gives a worked example, using a sample code area.

In that example a $250,000 property less a $125,000 homeowner's exemption leaves $125,000 taxable, and $125,000 times 0.014062635 comes to $1,757.83. This is an illustration from the county, not a rate for your address. Levy rates are certified by the state by the end of October, and the Treasurer posts the current list.

Your own figures are on the notice. The Assessor's assessment information page explains each line.

sections.h2: What is the Canyon County appeal process?
sections.html:
An appeal starts with an informal review and, if that fails, goes to the Board of Equalization by the fourth Monday in June. Idaho allows appeals of assessments only, not of taxes.

  • Grounds one: the property record is wrong, such as one bath instead of two, a carport recorded as a garage or 1,600 square feet recorded as 2,000.
  • Grounds two: the market value is too high, shown by similar properties that sold for less before January 1 of the current year.
  • Informal review: a meeting, call or email with the deputy assessor assigned to your area. A corrected notice usually follows within two to three weeks.
  • Formal appeal: a written form obtained from the person who conducted the review, filed under Idaho Code 63-501A.

Only arm's-length sales that closed before January 1 count, and sales after that date are not admissible. If you lose, further appeals go to the Idaho Board of Tax Appeals and then district court under Idaho Code 63-511. A hardship exemption application for the current year is also due June 20 and goes to the Board of Equalization.

sections.h2: When are Canyon County property taxes due, and what are the penalties?
sections.html:
Notices are mailed by the fourth Monday in November. The first half is due December 20 and the second half June 20 of the next year. The Treasurer says unpaid amounts accrue penalty and interest of 12% annually starting January 1.

The county also describes a 2% late charge on a first half not paid by December 20, with interest of 1% per month from January 1 on the tax and the charge. A returned check costs $20, and the county reports no formal monthly payment plan.

Two cases differ. Personal property and manufactured housing become fully delinquent if the first half is unpaid on December 20, and the entire tax is due. New construction produces a second, supplemental notice, mailed in March or April, with the full amount due June 20, prorated from the date of occupancy or completion to December 31 of the prior year.

The Treasurer adds that not receiving a tax notice does not excuse the tax, late charge or interest, citing Idaho Code 63-902(9). Anyone who bought property during the year and did not get a bill should call the office.

sections.h2: Which Canyon County programs reduce a bill?
sections.html:
Three programs, all run through the Assessor, can lower the bill. The homeowner's exemption halves the taxable value of an owner-occupied home and up to an acre of land, to a maximum the state lists as $125,000 for 2021 through 2025.

  • Property Tax Reduction (Circuit Breaker): income based, applications January 1 through April 15.
  • Veterans Property Tax Benefit: for 100% service-connected disabled veterans, up to $1,500 off the bill on a primary residence and up to an acre; same January 1 to April 15 window.
  • Homeowner Tax Relief credit: applied to properties with a homeowner's exemption in effect before the second Monday in July.

The county notes that relief programs have shifted year to year, and that an Additional Tax Relief credit available in 2023 was not offered for 2024. Check the Treasurer's page for the current year before relying on a figure. See also the state's homeowner's exemption page.

sections.h2: What do Canyon County sellers dealing with a tax problem usually face?
sections.html:
The common problems are a missed December deadline, an inherited house nobody is paying on, and a supplemental new-construction bill that arrives after a sale is already planned. Interest at 12% a year makes a late first half grow quickly.

We buy houses as is in Canyon County, so a seller with a delinquent balance does not have to repair or clean the house before an offer. Any unpaid tax is settled through escrow at closing, and the title company can give an exact payoff.

Call or text for a written cash offer on a Canyon County house. If you decline it, you owe us nothing.

faqs.q: When is the Canyon County appeal deadline?
faqs.a: The deadline to appeal assessed values on the regular roll is the fourth Monday in June, under Idaho Code 63-501A. Begin with an informal review before that date.

faqs.q: What is the Canyon County late fee for property tax?
faqs.a: A 2% late charge is added to an unpaid first half, and interest runs at 1% per month from January 1, which the county also describes as 12% annually.

faqs.q: Can I pay Canyon County property tax in installments?
faqs.a: Yes, in two halves: December 20 and June 20. The county says there is no formal monthly payment plan.

faqs.q: Can I appeal because my taxes are too high?
faqs.a: No. Idaho allows appeals of the assessed value only. Complaints about budgets go to the elected officials who set them.

faqs.q: Do I need to pay Canyon County taxes if I never got a notice?
faqs.a: Yes. The Treasurer cites Idaho Code 63-902(9): not receiving a notice does not excuse the tax, late charge or interest.
